question: Vasco da Gama reached which Indian port in May 1498?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Calicut.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Vasco da Gama landed at Calicut on 20 May 1498 after rounding the Cape of Good Hope in November 1497, opening the direct sea route from Europe to India (वास्को डी गामा 1498 में कालीकट पहुँचा)

 

• The ruler of Calicut at that time was the Zamorin, who allowed the Portuguese to trade in pepper and spices.

 

• Gama was guided across the Arabian Sea from East Africa with the help of a Gujarati pilot, Abdul Majid.

 

• His arrival made the Portuguese the first European power to establish contact with India by sea in the modern period.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Gama returned to Portugal in 1499 and visited India again in 1502 with a stronger fleet.

 

• The voyage was sponsored by King Manuel I of Portugal, and Gama's cargo of spices repaid the cost many times over.

 

• Bartolomeu Dias had earlier reached the Cape (1487), and Pedro Alvares Cabral set up the first Portuguese factory at Calicut in 1500.

 

NOTE

 

• Cochin (Option 1): Cochin became a Portuguese ally and early base under the Raja of Cochin, but it was not where Gama first landed; he anchored near Calicut and dealt with the Zamorin.

 

• Goa (Option 3): Goa was seized by Albuquerque only in 1510 from the Bijapur Sultan, twelve years after Gama's voyage, so it cannot be the port of his first landing.

 

• Surat (Option 4): Surat in Gujarat later became the English gateway (factory in 1613) and a French base in 1668; it had no role in Gama's first voyage.

question: Who was the ruler of Calicut when Vasco da Gama arrived in India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Zamorin.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Hindu ruler of Calicut in 1498 bore the title Zamorin (Samuthiri), and Gama presented himself at his court to seek trading rights (1498 में कालीकट का शासक ज़मोरिन था)

 

• Calicut was then the leading spice port on the Malabar Coast, frequented by Arab merchants who resented Portuguese competition.

 

• Relations soon soured because Arab traders influenced the Zamorin, and Portuguese ships later bombarded Calicut.

 

• The Zamorin remained a rival of the Portuguese, who turned to Cochin for support.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Cochin's ruler gave the Portuguese their first fort at Cochin (Fort Manuel) in 1503.

 

• The Portuguese tried to monopolise pepper exports from Malabar, and Calicut resisted their cartaze demands for decades.

 

• Kunjali Marakkars, naval chiefs of the Zamorin, fought the Portuguese through the sixteenth century.

 

• Portuguese relations with Calicut worsened in 1500 when Cabral's factory there was attacked, leading to bombardment of the city by Gama in 1502.

 

NOTE

 

• Krishnadevaraya (Option 1): Krishnadevaraya ruled Vijayanagara (1509-29) and dealt with the Portuguese on the west coast for horses, but he was not the king of Calicut at Gama's arrival.

 

• Adil Shah (Option 2): Adil Shah was the title of the Bijapur Sultans, from whom Albuquerque captured Goa in 1510; Bijapur had no authority over Calicut.

 

• Raja of Cochin (Option 3): The Raja of Cochin became an ally of the Portuguese because he was a rival of the Zamorin, which is why he cannot be the ruler Gama first met.

question: Which Indian merchant helped Vasco da Gama in reaching Calicut?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Abdul Majid.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Gujarati merchant Abdul Majid is traditionally said to have piloted Gama's ships from Malindi on the East African coast to Calicut in 1498 (गुजराती व्यापारी अब्दुल मजीद ने गामा को कालीकट पहुँचाया)

 

• Gujarati traders were skilled in monsoon navigation, so such a guide could cross the Arabian Sea directly.

 

• The voyage thus linked European Atlantic exploration with the old Indian Ocean trade network.

 

• Abdul Majid is named in standard textbooks as an Indian helper, which is why the question asks for an Indian merchant.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Gama's route ran from Lisbon to the Cape of Good Hope (22 Nov 1497), Malindi, and then Calicut on 20 May 1498.

 

• Gujarat, with ports such as Cambay and Surat, was the main centre of India's western maritime trade.

 

• Some authors identify the pilot as Ahmad ibn Majid of Arabia, but SSC follows the Abdul Majid version.

 

NOTE

 

• Ibn Battuta (Option 1): Ibn Battuta was a Moroccan traveller who visited India in the fourteenth century under Muhammad bin Tughluq, about a century and a half before the Portuguese arrival.

 

• Ahmad ibn Majid (Option 3): Ahmad ibn Majid was an Arab navigator and author of nautical texts; he is not an Indian merchant, and the textbook tradition does not name him for this voyage.

 

• Mulla Qutb (Option 4): Mulla Qutb Shah appears in history as a Deccan-linked figure and has no connection with Gama's voyage or the Malabar route.

question: Who was the first Portuguese Viceroy in India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Francisco de Almeida.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Francisco de Almeida (1505-09) was the first Portuguese Viceroy in India, appointed to protect Portuguese trading interests in the East (भारत में पहला पुर्तगाली वायसराय फ्रांसिस्को डी अल्मेडा था)

 

• He believed in naval power rather than land empire, a strategy known as the Blue Water Policy.

 

• His son Lourenco was killed in 1508 at Chaul fighting a Mamluk-Gujarat fleet, and Almeida avenged this at the Battle of Diu (1509).

 

• In 1509 he was succeeded by Albuquerque.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Battle of Diu (1509) gave the Portuguese control of the Arabian Sea against the combined fleet of Egypt, Gujarat and Calicut.

 

• Almeida's tenure (1505-1509) is the shortest of the three main early governors listed in textbooks.

 

• The title Viceroy was used after Almeida; before him Portuguese officials ruled as Captain-Majors.

 

NOTE

 

• Alfonso de Albuquerque (Option 1): Alfonso de Albuquerque succeeded Almeida in 1509 and is regarded as the real founder of Portuguese power; he was the second governor, not the first.

 

• Nino da Cunha (Option 2): Nino da Cunha governed from 1529 to 1538 and shifted the capital from Cochin to Goa; he came more than two decades after Almeida.

 

• Vasco da Gama (Option 4): Vasco da Gama discovered the sea route and came back as Viceroy only in 1524, dying at Cochin the same year, so he was not the first holder of the office.

question: The 'Blue Water Policy' in the Indian Ocean was associated with which Portuguese governor?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Francisco de Almeida.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Francisco de Almeida pursued the Blue Water Policy, which sought Portuguese supremacy through control of the seas rather than through land possessions (ब्लू वाटर पॉलिसी — फ्रांसिस्को डी अल्मेडा की नौसैनिक नीति)

 

• Under this policy the Portuguese used a fleet to dominate the Indian Ocean and to force other ships to take a pass called the cartaze.

 

• The policy relied on strong forts at coastal points and on defeating rivals such as the Egyptian-Gujarati fleet at Diu in 1509.

 

• It differed from his successor's approach, which stressed territorial bases like Goa.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The cartaze was a naval pass or licence that Indian and Arab ships had to buy from the Portuguese.

 

• Albuquerque abandoned the pure naval approach and encouraged Portuguese settlement and marriage with local women.

 

• Portuguese sea control through the sixteenth century made them known as masters of the Indian Ocean.

 

NOTE

 

• Alfonso de Albuquerque (Option 2): Albuquerque is remembered for acquiring Goa and building a territorial base, which is the opposite of an approach limited to sea power alone.

 

• Nino da Cunha (Option 3): Nino da Cunha is known for moving the capital to Goa in 1530 and setting up the Hooghly factory, not for the Blue Water Policy.

 

• Joao de Castro (Option 4): Joao de Castro was a later Viceroy (1545-48) who is known for fighting at Diu and for his reputation for honesty; textbooks do not link him with this policy.

question: Who is regarded as the real founder of Portuguese power in India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Alfonso de Albuquerque.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Alfonso de Albuquerque (governor 1509-15) is considered the real founder of Portuguese power in India because he built a lasting territorial and administrative base (पुर्तगाली सत्ता का वास्तविक संस्थापक अल्फांसो डी अल्बुकर्क)

 

• He took charge in 1509, when Cochin was the seat of Portuguese power.

 

• In 1510 he captured Goa from the Bijapur Sultan, which became the headquarters of the Portuguese empire in the East.

 

• He also encouraged intermarriage between Portuguese soldiers and Indian women to build a loyal settler community.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Albuquerque also conquered Malacca (1511) and Hormuz (1515), strengthening Portuguese control of trade routes.

 

• He died at sea near Goa in 1515.

 

• Goa remained the capital of Portuguese India until 1961, when it was merged into the Indian Union.

 

• Albuquerque's portrait of a tough but fair administrator made him respected even among some local people in Goa, where he abolished sati in 1510.

 

NOTE

 

• Francisco de Almeida (Option 1): Francisco de Almeida was the first Viceroy and relied mainly on naval strength; his policy did not create a land base, so he is not called the real founder.

 

• Vasco da Gama (Option 2): Vasco da Gama opened the sea route in 1498, but he was an explorer who made short visits, and he did not build the administrative structure of the empire.

 

• Nino da Cunha (Option 3): Nino da Cunha moved the capital to Goa in 1530, after Albuquerque had already captured it; he developed rather than founded Portuguese rule.

question: In which year did the Portuguese capture Goa from the Sultan of Bijapur?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1510.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Alfonso de Albuquerque captured Goa in 1510 from the Adil Shahi Sultan of Bijapur, giving the Portuguese their first major territorial possession (1510 में अल्बुकर्क ने बीजापुर से गोवा जीता)

 

• Goa's harbour on the Konkan coast and its horse trade with the Deccan made it valuable.

 

• Albuquerque was appointed governor in 1509 and soon after seized the island with local help.

 

• Goa became the capital of Portuguese possessions in 1530 and remained so until 1961.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Panaji, the present capital of Goa, is also linked in textbooks with Portuguese settlement after 1510.

 

• The Portuguese carried the first printing press to India at Goa in 1556.

 

• Goa's Inquisition, started in 1560, is among the best-known features of Portuguese rule.

 

• Bijapur was ruled by the Adil Shahi dynasty, whose Sultan Yusuf Adil Shah had earlier held Goa, and Albuquerque took it first in February 1510, lost it, and finally held it in November 1510.

 

NOTE

 

• 1498 (Option 1): 1498 is the year of Vasco da Gama's arrival at Calicut, not the year Goa was acquired. The Portuguese landing of that year was on the Malabar coast, far south of Goa.

 

• 1530 (Option 2): 1530 is the year Nino da Cunha shifted the capital from Cochin to Goa; the conquest itself had happened twenty years earlier.

 

• 1535 (Option 4): 1535 is close to the period when the Portuguese gained Diu rights and Hooghly interests, but it is not the date of the capture of Goa.

question: Which Portuguese governor transferred the capital from Cochin to Goa in 1530?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Nino da Cunha.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Nino da Cunha (governor 1529-38) shifted the Portuguese capital from Cochin to Goa in 1530 (1530 में नीनो दा कुन्हा ने राजधानी कोचीन से गोवा स्थानांतरित की)

 

• He also established a Portuguese factory at Hooghly in Bengal, extending their trade towards the east.

 

• Goa already belonged to the Portuguese since 1510, so his step formalised its status as the administrative centre.

 

• From then on Goa remained the capital of Portuguese India till its liberation in 1961.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Cunha acquired Bassein and Diu rights from Bahadur Shah of Gujarat in the 1530s.

 

• Hooghly later became a notable Portuguese settlement until Shah Jahan expelled them in 1632.

 

• The Portuguese capital was thus first Cochin (1505-1530), then Goa.

 

• Cochin had been the first capital, where the Portuguese built Fort Manuel in 1503 with the consent of its Raja.

 

NOTE

 

• Alfonso de Albuquerque (Option 1): Albuquerque conquered Goa in 1510 but kept Cochin as the main seat during his own tenure; the transfer of the capital came later.

 

• Francisco de Almeida (Option 2): Almeida governed from Cochin in 1505-09 and never made Goa the capital, since it was not in Portuguese hands during his time.

 

• Pedro Alvares Cabral (Option 3): Pedro Alvares Cabral reached Calicut in 1500 and founded a factory there, but he was a navigator and never held the capital-shifting authority of a governor.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Battle of Swally (1612):

1. It was fought between the English and the Portuguese.

2. The English fleet was led by Captain Thomas Best.

3. The English were defeated in this battle.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: the Battle of Swally (Suvali) in 1612, off the Gujarat coast near Surat, was a naval clash between the English and the Portuguese (सुवाली का युद्ध 1612 — अंग्रेज बनाम पुर्तगाली)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: the English ships were commanded by Captain Thomas Best.

 

• Statement 3 is incorrect: the English won, and the victory showed that the Portuguese could be challenged at sea.

 

• As a result the English replaced the Portuguese as the leading European power in Indian trade and set up a factory at Surat in 1613.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The victory persuaded Mughal officials at Surat that the English were a useful counterweight to the Portuguese.

 

• Portuguese power in India had begun to decline after about 1600.

 

• Swally, the roadstead of Surat, was a safe anchorage for ships of the Company.

 

• Swally lies at the mouth of the Tapti near Surat, and the encounter is sometimes also called the Battle of Suvali.

 

NOTE

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 1): Combining statements 2 and 3 fails because statement 3 is false; Thomas Best won the encounter, so the English were not defeated.

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 3): Pairing statements 1 and 3 is wrong for the same reason: the first part is true, but the outcome claimed in statement 3 was the reverse of history.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Accepting all three statements would include the false claim of an English defeat, which contradicts the result that gave the Company its position at Surat.

question: Which of the following was NOT introduced to India by the Portuguese?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Tea.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Tea was not brought by the Portuguese; its commercial cultivation in India began under the British, with the Assam plantations in the 1830s (चाय पुर्तगालियों ने नहीं, अंग्रेज़ों ने भारत में उगाई)

 

• The Portuguese introduced several American crops: Potato, Tobacco, Maize and Red Chilli.

 

• Other Portuguese-linked items include the cashew nut, pineapple and papaya, which spread from the Goa-Malabar region.

 

• These crops reached India from the Americas through the Columbian exchange carried by Portuguese ships.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The first Indian tea gardens were set up in Assam after the discovery of the indigenous Assam tea plant by Robert Bruce.

 

• Chilli quickly replaced black pepper in many Indian cuisines.

 

• Tobacco reached the Mughal court in Akbar's reign; Jahangir later tried to ban smoking.

 

• Potato was introduced in Western India by the Portuguese and spread across the Gangetic plain under British encouragement in the nineteenth century.

 

NOTE

 

• Potato (Option 1): The potato came from the Americas to India through Portuguese traders, and it later spread widely under the British, so it is a valid Portuguese introduction.

 

• Tobacco (Option 2): Tobacco was brought by the Portuguese in the sixteenth century and reached the Mughal court soon after; it therefore does not answer the NOT question.

 

• Maize (Option 3): Maize, a New World crop, was also introduced by the Portuguese, and it became a staple in several hill and tribal regions.

question: Bombay came into English hands as dowry on the marriage of Charles II with which Portuguese princess?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Catherine of Braganza.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Charles II of England married Catherine of Braganza of Portugal in 1662 and received Bombay as part of her dowry (कैथरीन ऑफ ब्रगांज़ा के दहेज में बम्बई अंग्रेज़ों को मिला)

 

• The two were betrothed in 1661 and married in 1662, which is why textbooks quote 1661-62.

 

• The marriage was a political alliance of England and Portugal against Spain and the Dutch.

 

• Charles II found Bombay costly to hold and in 1668 leased it to the East India Company.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The annual rent fixed in 1668 was just ten pounds, payable in gold.

 

• Bombay became the Company's western headquarters after Gerald Aungier shifted it from Surat in the 1670s.

 

• Bombay, Madras and Calcutta formed the three presidency towns of British India.

 

• Catherine of Braganza was the daughter of King John IV of Portugal, and the marriage treaty also gave England Tangier.

 

NOTE

 

• Isabella of Castile (Option 1): Isabella of Castile was a Spanish queen of the fifteenth century who sponsored Columbus; she had no link with Charles II or Bombay.

 

• Mary of Burgundy (Option 3): Mary of Burgundy belonged to the Habsburg line of the late fifteenth century and cannot be connected with a seventeenth-century English royal wedding.

 

• Maria Theresa (Option 4): Maria Theresa was an eighteenth-century Habsburg empress of Austria, who ruled long after Charles II's marriage and had no role in Bombay's transfer.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Portuguese in India:

1. After the seventeenth century they retained only Goa, Diu and Daman.

2. Their rule in Goa lasted until 1961.

3. The Portuguese factory at Hooghly in Bengal was set up by Albuquerque.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: after the Dutch and English attacked their trade, the Portuguese were reduced to Goa, Diu and Daman (केवल गोवा, दीव और दमन पुर्तगालियों के पास बचे)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: the Portuguese came first, stayed the longest and left only when these territories were taken over by India in 1961.

 

• Statement 3 is incorrect: the Hooghly factory was established under Nino da Cunha (1529-38), not Albuquerque, who died in 1515.

 

• Albuquerque is credited with the capture of Goa (1510), which is a different achievement.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• India's action to end Portuguese rule in Goa is known as Operation Vijay (December 1961).

 

• The Portuguese were expelled from Hooghly by Shah Jahan in 1632 after a siege.

 

• The Portuguese were the first to arrive (1498) and the last to leave, a point often asked in SSC papers.

 

• Daman and Diu lie on the Gujarat coast, while Goa lies on the Konkan coast, and all three were attached to the Union in 1961 as one Union Territory until Goa became a state in 1987.

 

NOTE

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 2): Joining statements 2 and 3 adds the false Hooghly claim; the factory is linked to Nino da Cunha's governorship, and statement 1 is also true but is left out of this pair.

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 3): Joining statements 1 and 3 repeats the same error about Albuquerque and leaves out the true 1961 statement, so the combination cannot be right.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Choosing all three would accept the claim about Albuquerque and Hooghly, though the Bengal factory was created about two decades after his death.

question: In which year was the Dutch East India Company established?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1602.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Dutch East India Company (VOC) was formed in 1602 by merging several Dutch trading companies, with a charter giving it monopoly rights in the East (डच ईस्ट इंडिया कंपनी की स्थापना 1602 में हुई)

 

• It was a joint-stock company that could wage war, make treaties and found colonies in the Asian trade.

 

• Its main base was at Batavia in Java, and in India it concentrated on spices and textiles of the Coromandel coast.

 

• Dutch voyages to the East had started earlier, with Cornelis de Houtman in 1596.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The VOC is often described as the world's first major joint-stock company.

 

• The English company (1600) preceded it by two years, and the French company (1664) came much later.

 

• The Dutch sold Indian textiles in Southeast Asia in exchange for spices.

 

• The VOC was authorised to recruit soldiers and build forts, which gave it quasi-sovereign powers in Asia, and its main rival in India was the English company.

 

NOTE

 

• 1596 (Option 1): 1596 is the year of Cornelis de Houtman's first voyage to Bantam in Java, before the company existed. Houtman's voyage was a preliminary expedition that inspired the creation of the company.

 

• 1605 (Option 2): 1605 marks the first Dutch factory in India, at Masulipatnam, which came three years after the company's formation. That date is the first Dutch factory, a step that followed the formation of the company.

 

• 1664 (Option 4): 1664 is the year in which the French East India Company was founded under Colbert, not the Dutch one. That is the French company, set up by a minister of Louis XIV.

question: Where was the first Dutch factory in India established in 1605?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Masulipatnam.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Dutch set up their first Indian factory in 1605 at Masulipatnam on the Coromandel (Andhra) coast, where cotton textiles were available (डचों की पहली भारतीय फैक्ट्री 1605 में मसूलीपट्टनम में)

 

• Masulipatnam was a major port of the Golconda kingdom and attracted European traders for its painted cloth.

 

• The Dutch later moved their Coromandel headquarters to Pulicat.

 

• The English also opened their first temporary factory in India at Masulipatnam in 1611.

 

• The Dutch took their Coromandel headquarters to Pulicat in 1609, building Fort Geldria, and they traded in cotton goods, indigo and saltpetre.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Pulicat had the Fort Geldria, built by the Dutch in 1609.

 

• Dutch settlements also included Chinsurah in Bengal, Nagapattinam and Cochin in the south.

 

• The Dutch defeated the Portuguese at Cochin in 1663 and took over their Malabar possessions.

 

• Masulipatnam, also called Machilipatnam, was the chief port of the Golconda sultanate and was famed for its kalamkari cloth.

 

NOTE

 

• Pulicat (Option 1): Pulicat became the main Dutch centre on the Coromandel after 1609, but Masulipatnam was the first factory, established four years earlier.

 

• Surat (Option 3): Surat was where the English set up the permanent factory in 1613 and where the French followed in 1668; the first Dutch post was elsewhere.

 

• Chinsurah (Option 4): Chinsurah in Bengal was a later Dutch settlement on the Hooghly, developed in the seventeenth century, not the first Dutch factory.

question: Who was the first Dutchman to reach the East Indies (Bantam, Java) in 1596?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Cornelis de Houtman.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Cornelis de Houtman was the first Dutchman to reach the East Indies, landing at Bantam in Java in 1596 (1596 में कॉर्नेलिस डी हाउटमैन बन्तम पहुँचने वाला पहला डच)

 

• His voyage showed Dutch merchants that spices could be bought directly in Asia without Portuguese middlemen at Lisbon.

 

• It led to the creation of many small trading companies, which merged into the Dutch East India Company in 1602.

 

• Dutch voyages to India followed soon after his expedition.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Houtman's route used knowledge gained from Dutch navigator Jan Huyghen van Linschoten, who worked at Goa.

 

• The Dutch later dominated the spice trade of Indonesia from their capital Batavia.

 

• In India, they were mostly interested in cotton and indigo, along with saltpetre from Bihar.

 

• Houtman's voyage of 1595-97 sailed with four ships from Texel and lost nearly two-thirds of its crew, but the spice cargo still made a profit.

 

NOTE

 

• Vasco da Gama (Option 1): Vasco da Gama was Portuguese and reached India by sea in 1498; he had nothing to do with Dutch voyages to Java.

 

• Thomas Best (Option 2): Thomas Best was an English captain who defeated the Portuguese at Swally in 1612, so he belongs to the British story.

 

• Francis Caron (Option 4): Francis Caron was a Dutch-born servant who joined the French and founded their first Indian factory at Surat in 1668, not the first Dutchman to reach Java.

question: Who was the first Englishman (merchant) to arrive at Akbar's court, in 1583?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ralph Fitch.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ralph Fitch was the first English merchant to arrive at the court of Akbar, around 1583, and he gave an account of his travels in India and Burma (1583 में राल्फ फिच अकबर के दरबार पहुँचने वाला पहला अंग्रेज़ व्यापारी)

 

• His account of the wealth of the East encouraged English merchants to form a company.

 

• He travelled with other English merchants and was jailed for a time by the Portuguese at Goa.

 

• John Mildenhall followed in 1599, but Fitch was earlier.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Fitch visited Agra and Fatehpur Sikri, then travelled on to Bengal and Burma.

 

• The English East India Company was formed on 31 December 1600 after the favourable reports of such travellers.

 

• Thomas Stevens, a Jesuit from England, was in Goa in 1579 but is not counted as a merchant.

 

• Fitch left an account that was later published by Richard Hakluyt in his Principal Navigations, which spread knowledge of India across England.

 

NOTE

 

• John Mildenhall (Option 2): John Mildenhall came to India in 1599 by the overland route, which is later than Fitch's arrival at Akbar's court.

 

• William Hawkins (Option 3): William Hawkins reached Surat in 1608 and the court of Jahangir in 1609, so he met Akbar's son rather than Akbar.

 

• Thomas Roe (Option 4): Sir Thomas Roe was James I's ambassador to Jahangir between 1615 and 1619, and he arrived long after Akbar's death in 1605.

question: Which English Queen granted the charter to the East India Company in 1600?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Elizabeth I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Queen Elizabeth I granted the royal charter on 31 December 1600 to a group of merchants known as the 'Merchant Adventurers', creating the East India Company (1600 में रानी एलिज़ाबेथ प्रथम ने चार्टर दिया)

 

• The charter gave the company a monopoly of English trade with the East for fifteen years.

 

• The company was formed after merchants saw the profits made by the Portuguese and Dutch in the spice trade.

 

• Its first voyages sailed to the Spice Islands before attention shifted to India.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The charter was later renewed by James I and by Charles II, with the monopoly made permanent in the seventeenth century.

 

• The company was known as 'John Company' in India.

 

• After 1858 the Crown took over from the East India Company following the Revolt of 1857.

 

• The early Company was headquartered in London at Leadenhall Street, and its governor and twenty-four committee members managed affairs.

 

NOTE

 

• Mary I (Option 1): Mary I ruled from 1553 to 1558, before the formation of the company, and she is better known for her Catholic restoration.

 

• Anne (Option 2): Queen Anne reigned from 1702 to 1714, and the Company's two rival bodies were merged in 1708 during her reign; she did not grant the original charter.

 

• Victoria (Option 3): Victoria reigned much later (1837-1901) and became Empress of India in 1876, which is after the company's creation by nearly three centuries.

question: William Hawkins came to India in 1608 as an envoy of the English company, travelling in which ship?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Hector.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Captain William Hawkins sailed in the ship Hector and reached Surat in 1608, then Jahangir's court in 1609 with a letter from King James I (हॉकिन्स हेक्टर जहाज़ से 1608 में सूरत पहुँचा)

 

• He sought permission to set up an English trading centre at Surat.

 

• Jahangir treated him well, giving him the title English Khan and a mansab of 400.

 

• The emperor first agreed but later refused because of Portuguese opposition at court.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Hawkins left the Mughal court in 1611 without getting the permission he wanted.

 

• Akbar had died in 1605, so Hawkins had to approach Jahangir.

 

• The English finally got Surat only after the victory at Swally and the efforts of Sir Thomas Roe.

 

• Hawkins had earlier served as a commander of the Company's ships and spoke Turkish, which he used to speak to Jahangir without an interpreter.

 

NOTE

 

• Golden Hind (Option 2): Golden Hind was the ship of Francis Drake, who circumnavigated the globe in the 1570s, and it had no link with the Company's mission to Jahangir.

 

• Red Dragon (Option 3): Red Dragon was the flagship of the first voyage of James Lancaster in 1601 to the East Indies, not the vessel that brought Hawkins to Surat.

 

• Mayflower (Option 4): Mayflower is famous for carrying the Pilgrim Fathers to North America in 1620 and was not part of the Company's embassy to the Mughal emperor.

question: Sir Thomas Roe, who got permission for English factories at Agra, Ahmedabad and Broach, was the ambassador of which English king?
solution_text:
The correct answer is James I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sir Thomas Roe came to Jahangir's court in 1615 as an ambassador of King James I and stayed there for about three years, up to 1619 (सर टॉमस रो इंग्लैंड के राजा जेम्स प्रथम का राजदूत था)

 

• He won permission for English factories at Agra, Ahmedabad, Baroda and Broach.

 

• Agra became the first inland factory of the Company.

 

• He achieved this by diplomacy rather than force and by giving gifts and appealing to Jahangir's interest in curiosities.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Roe's Mughal mission followed that of William Hawkins, who had failed in 1609-11.

 

• James I also gave the Company its early privileges beyond Elizabeth's charter.

 

• Roe's journal gives a detailed picture of the Mughal court under Jahangir.

 

• Roe's official task also included seeking a commercial treaty, but Jahangir refused a formal treaty and offered only farmans for particular factories.

 

NOTE

 

• Charles II (Option 1): Charles II reigned in the later seventeenth century and is known for receiving Bombay in 1662; he was not the king who sent Roe.

 

• Henry VIII (Option 3): Henry VIII ruled in the first half of the sixteenth century, well before the Company existed, so he could not have sent any envoy to Jahangir.

 

• George III (Option 4): George III was king in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, the time of the Anglo-French wars and Plassey, not Roe's mission.

question: The first permanent English factory in India was set up in 1613 at
solution_text:
The correct answer is Surat.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The English founded their first permanent factory at Surat in 1613, after Mughal permission and the naval success at Swally in 1612 (1613 में अंग्रेज़ों की पहली स्थायी फैक्ट्री सूरत में बनी)

 

• Surat was the leading port of the Mughal empire in Gujarat and a hub of trade with Persia, Arabia and Europe.

 

• The earlier temporary factory had been set up at Masulipatnam in 1611.

 

• Surat remained the main English centre till Bombay replaced it in the later seventeenth century.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Madras's Fort St George was built in 1639-40 by Francis Day with permission from a local ruler.

 

• Roe's efforts later brought factories at Agra, Ahmedabad, Baroda and Broach.

 

• The Mughals' friendship at Surat gave the English access to cotton goods of Gujarat.

 

• The Surat factory's success came with a farman from the Mughal governor of Gujarat, and in 1615 Roe also got a general permission from Jahangir.

 

NOTE

 

• Madras (Option 2): Madras was acquired much later, in 1639, when Francis Day obtained land on the Coromandel coast and built Fort St George there.

 

• Masulipatnam (Option 3): Masulipatnam had the temporary English factory of 1611, and the notes distinguish it as temporary, not as the first permanent one.

 

• Hooghly (Option 4): Hooghly saw the English factory only in 1651 and was located in Bengal; it was neither the first permanent factory nor established in 1613.

question: On the bank of which river was the first English factory in Bengal established in 1651?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Hugli.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The first English factory in Bengal was founded in 1651 on the bank of the river Hugli, a distributary of the Ganga (1651 में बंगाल की पहली अंग्रेज़ी फैक्ट्री हुगली नदी के किनारे)

 

• Shah Shuja, Aurangzeb's brother and then governor of Bengal, allowed the English free trade in the province.

 

• The Hugli became the lifeline of English commerce, and the later settlement of Calcutta also stood on its banks.

 

• Portuguese Hooghly lay on the same river and had been an earlier European trading station.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Shah Shuja's grant gave the English trade for an annual payment of 3,000 rupees.

 

• Job Charnock founded Calcutta (1690) on the same river, and Fort William was built there in 1696-1700.

 

• The Kaveri is linked to Tanjore and Tranquebar, while the Mahanadi flows through Odisha.

 

• Before the Hugli factory, the English had obtained permission in 1633 to trade at Hariharpur and Balasore on the Odisha coast.

 

NOTE

 

• Ganga at Patna (Option 1): The Ganga at Patna was a Bihar trade centre for saltpetre, but the 1651 Bengal factory was founded on the Hugli, not at Patna.

 

• Kaveri (Option 3): Kaveri flows through Tamil Nadu, where the Danes built Tranquebar and the Dutch sat at Nagapattinam, so it is far from the Bengal factory.

 

• Mahanadi (Option 4): Mahanadi is the river of Odisha, and while the English had early posts in Balasore and Hariharpur there, the 1651 factory was in Bengal.

question: In 1668 King Charles II leased Bombay to the East India Company for an annual rent of
solution_text:
The correct answer is 10 pounds.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Charles II leased Bombay to the East India Company in 1668 for just 10 pounds a year, since it was a costly and unprofitable possession for the Crown (1668 में बम्बई कंपनी को 10 पाउंड वार्षिक पर दी गई)

 

• The island had come to him in 1662 as the dowry of Catherine of Braganza.

 

• Under the Company, Bombay's excellent harbour and defensive position made it better than Surat as a base.

 

• Gerald Aungier later developed it into the Company's western headquarters.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Bombay later became one of the three presidencies, along with Madras and Calcutta.

 

• The rent was a token sum, reflecting that the Crown wanted the Company to bear the cost of defence and administration.

 

• Portuguese settlers on the island had resisted the transfer, but the English established control by 1665-68.

 

• Surat's decline, after Shivaji sacked it in 1664 and 1670, also pushed the Company towards shifting its western base to Bombay.

 

NOTE

 

• 100 pounds (Option 1): A rent of 100 pounds is ten times too large; the record says the lease was only a token amount.

 

• 1,000 pounds (Option 2): A rent of 1,000 pounds would have made the island a heavy burden, and the lease was in fact made to relieve the Crown, not to collect large revenue.

 

• 10,000 pounds (Option 4): A figure of 10,000 pounds is far beyond the modest rent; the symbolic payment of ten pounds a year was what the Company paid.

question: Fort William, built at Kolkata, was declared the first British Presidency city in India in
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1700.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Fort William at Calcutta (Kolkata) was declared the first Presidency city of the British in India in 1700 (1700 में फोर्ट विलियम पहला ब्रिटिश प्रेसीडेंसी नगर घोषित हुआ)

 

• Its first governor (president) was Charles Eyre, under whom the settlement acquired a fort and administration.

 

• Calcutta joined Bombay and Madras as the three presidency towns of English settlements in India.

 

• The settlement had grown from the site of Sutanuti, where Job Charnock had set up a factory in 1690.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The English acquired the zamindari of three villages (Sutanuti, Kalikata, Govindpur) in 1698.

 

• Calcutta was captured by Siraj-ud-Daulah in 1756 and retaken by Clive in 1757.

 

• Calcutta served as the capital of British India until 1911.

 

• The Company's early presidency structure had a president and council, which was later called a governor and council.

 

NOTE

 

• 1639 (Option 2): 1639 is when Fort St George was founded at Madras by Francis Day, not when Fort William was given presidency rank.

 

• 1690 (Option 3): 1690 is the year when Job Charnock set up the settlement at Sutanuti; the presidency status came a decade later. That event is linked to Calcutta's origin as a trading settlement.

 

• 1757 (Option 4): 1757 is the year of the Battle of Plassey, a political event that came long after the settlement had become a presidency city.

question: The first factory of the Danes in India was founded at
solution_text:
The correct answer is Tranquebar.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Danes founded their first Indian factory in 1620 at Tranquebar (Tharangambadi) on the Tamil Nadu coast, after the Danish East India Company was set up in 1616 (डेनिश कंपनी की पहली फैक्ट्री 1620 में ट्रांकेबार)

 

• Tranquebar remained the chief Danish port in the south for over two centuries.

 

• The Danes later added a colony at Serampore in Bengal in 1755, which became their headquarters.

 

• Their business never grew large because of limited support from their government.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Tranquebar also hosted the first Protestant mission in India, led by Bartholomew Ziegenbalg in 1706.

 

• The Danes were the fourth European power to come to India, after Portuguese, Dutch and English.

 

• The Danish fort at Tranquebar, Fort Dansborg, still stands.

 

• The Danish Company's Tranquebar settlement was gained from the Nayak of Tanjore through a treaty in 1620, which also allowed them to build Fort Dansborg.

 

NOTE

 

• Serampore (Option 1): Serampore was acquired in 1755, over a century after Tranquebar, and became a headquarters in Bengal rather than the first Danish factory.

 

• Pondicherry (Option 2): Pondicherry was founded by the French in 1674 under Francois Martin, so it belongs to a different European company. It was acquired in the Coromandel region after the Danes were already at Tranquebar.

 

• Masulipatnam (Option 3): Masulipatnam was the first Dutch factory in 1605 and an English temporary factory in 1611, not a Danish one. The Danes were never based there; the port served other companies.

question: The headquarters of the Danes in India was the colony at
solution_text:
The correct answer is Serampore.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In 1755 the Danes established a colony at Serampore in West Bengal on the Hugli, which became their headquarters in India (1755 में डेन लोगों ने सीरामपुर को अपना मुख्यालय बनाया)

 

• Their original base was Tranquebar, but Bengal's rich trade made Serampore more useful.

 

• Serampore later became famous for the Baptist Mission with William Carey and for the Serampore College.

 

• In 1845 the Danes sold all their Indian settlements to the British.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Serampore College, founded in 1818, was among the earliest institutions of higher education in modern India.

 

• The Serampore Mission Press printed books and Bengali newspapers, such as Samachar Darpan (1818).

 

• The Danish settlement at Serampore was bought by the British in 1845 together with Tranquebar.

 

• Serampore is also remembered as Fredricksnagore, its Danish name, and it fell to the British in 1801 temporarily during the Napoleonic wars before the final sale.

 

NOTE

 

• Tranquebar (Option 1): Tranquebar was the first Danish factory (1620) in the south, but the notes point to Serampore as the headquarters after 1755.

 

• Chandernagore (Option 3): Chandernagore on the Hugli was a French settlement, which Clive captured in 1757; it was not Danish. It stayed under French rule until 1954 and was never a Danish possession.

 

• Mahe (Option 4): Mahe on the Malabar coast was a French possession as well, retained by France until 1954, so it cannot be the Danish centre.
